title: Noun phrases and quantity: cumulative review
objectives: Build simple noun phrases in a natural order.
Use partitive expressions with uncountable nouns.
Review quantifiers, relative clauses and passive forms.

explanation.heading: Meaning and use
paragraphs: A noun phrase is a group of words built around a noun. In ‘those two interesting books’, books is the main noun. Those points to the books, two gives the number, and interesting describes them. A noun phrase can be the subject or object of a sentence: ‘Those two books are useful’ and ‘I borrowed those two books’.

A determiner is a word such as a, the, this, my or those that helps identify or limit a noun. A singular countable noun normally needs a determiner: ‘a book’, ‘the book’ or ‘my book’. We do not normally combine two central determiners directly before the same noun: say ‘my book’ or ‘the book’, not ‘the my book’.

explanation.heading: Form
paragraphs: The usual order in a simple noun phrase is determiner, number or quantity, adjective, noun: ‘the three new chairs’ or ‘some useful information’. An adjective before a noun normally has the same form with singular and plural nouns: ‘a new chair’ and ‘new chairs’. The noun's countability determines which quantifiers fit: many chairs but much information.

Use a unit or container to count an amount of an uncountable noun: ‘a piece of information’, ‘two pieces of information’ and ‘three bottles of water’. The unit word becomes plural when necessary; the uncountable noun normally stays the same. Use of in these expressions.

explanation.heading: Examples in context
paragraphs: Compare ‘some books’ with ‘some of the books’. Some books introduces an unspecified number of books; some of the books selects from a particular group already identified by the context. Likewise, ‘a few students’ is general, while ‘a few of the students’ selects from a known group. Of is needed in these examples before the determiner the.

This unit reviews quantifiers and related structures. ‘Each student has a ticket’ uses a singular noun and verb. ‘The people who have tickets may enter’ uses a defining relative clause to identify which people. ‘The tickets were checked’ uses a past passive to focus on the tickets.

explanation.heading: Contrasts and common mistakes
paragraphs: Do not add -s to an adjective just because the noun is plural: ‘three new chairs’, not ‘three news chairs’. Do not add a plural ending to information in its usual uncountable meaning: say ‘two pieces of information’, not ‘two informations’. Some words have different countable and uncountable meanings, so a dictionary and context remain useful.

Not every group of words before a noun follows only the simple pattern taught here. Other modifiers can occur, and some determiners combine in particular structures, such as ‘all the students’. The examples in this unit give a practical starting point for ordinary noun phrases and partitive expressions.

examples.sentence: Those two interesting books are useful.
examples.note: The phrase has a determiner, number, adjective and noun.
A introduces a singular countable noun.
Information is uncountable in this meaning.

examples.sentence: Two pieces of information were missing.
examples.note: Pieces is the plural unit; information stays uncountable.

examples.sentence: Some of the books are new.
examples.note: Of the books selects from an identified group.

examples.sentence: A few students stayed after class.
examples.note: A few introduces a small countable number.
Each student is singular in this pattern.

examples.sentence: The tickets were checked at the door.
examples.note: Were checked is a past passive with a plural subject.

common_errors.reason: Do not combine the and my directly before the noun.

common_errors.correct: We need two pieces of information.
common_errors.reason: Use a plural unit with uncountable information.
The adjective does not take a plural ending.

summary: A simple noun phrase can contain a determiner, a quantity, an adjective and a noun.
Use a unit such as a piece of to count an uncountable noun.
Use of before the identified group in expressions such as some of the books.
